title: Kahola: beyond hunger, grief and death
hookLine: the next challenger asks the very same question, word for word, and hears why some Hindus give everything up
carry: the self is beyond hunger, grief and death
tomorrow: a woman stands up among the men. how far will her why go?
last: THE SELF IS THE SELF IS THE SEER, NEVER THE SEEN, NEVER THE SEEN.

lines: THE SAME QUESTION, WORD FOR WORD.
cards: Here's something odd about this debate. The next man to stand up, Kahola, asks exactly the same question Ushasta just asked, word for word: explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, the self within all.
You'd expect Yajnavalkya to say: I just answered that. He doesn't. He answers again, from a completely different side.
Yesterday the self was the seer you can't see. Today it's what's left when hunger, grief and death have nothing to hold on to.

teach.b: That is your self, within all, Yajnavalkya says. Which one? The one beyond hunger and thirst, beyond grief and confusion, beyond old age and death.
Three pairs. Hunger and thirst belong to the body. Grief and confusion belong to the mind.
Old age and death belong to a life. Tradition calls these six the waves, rising and falling on the surface while the depth stays still. Then Yajnavalkya says what knowing this does to people.
Knowing this self, the wise give up wanting sons, wanting wealth, wanting worlds, and live by begging.

teach.h: WANTING SONS, WEALTH, WORLDS: JUST WANTING.
teach.b: Wanting sons is really wanting wealth; wanting wealth is really wanting worlds. Both are just wanting.
This is the root of sannyasa, renunciation: in Hindu life, some people take a vow, put on ochre cloth and set the wanting down, because they're looking for a self no wave can touch.
Most Hindus never take that vow, and the tradition honors householders too. Then a surprising ladder.

teach.h: AFTER LEARNING, LIVE LIKE A CHILD.
teach.b: Having finished with learning, one should want to live like a child; past that, one becomes a muni, a silent sage.
After all those years of memorizing the Veda, the next step is the plainness of a child. Some hear simplicity in that word, balya; Shankara reads it as the strength that knowledge gives.
Either way, the scholars who came to win cows with their learning are told it's a stage, not the summit. And Kahola falls silent.

how: Hindu renunciants, sannyasis, take vows giving up the desires for family, wealth and worlds that Yajnavalkya names here; Vedanta teachers speak of the six waves of hunger, thirst, grief, confusion, old age and death as what the self is beyond.

o: the man who asked Ushasta's question again
the scholar who won the thousand cows
the sage who took a vow of silence

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.

s: Kahola asks a different question from Ushasta
word for word the same. Yajnavalkya answers from a different side.
Yajnavalkya says wanting sons and wanting wealth are both just wanting
wanting sons is wanting wealth; wanting wealth is wanting worlds.
in this ladder, learning is the final step
after learning comes childlikeness, then the silent sage.

games.q: you've spent years memorizing the Veda and you've finished. according to Yajnavalkya, what comes next?
o: more learning, in a harder school.
games.why: having finished with learning, one should want to live like a child. then, past both, one becomes a muni, a silent sage.

practice: For now, set down everything you know, the Sanskrit words, the arguments, the names, and let them rest on the floor beside you. Look at the room the way a small child would: shapes, light, sound, no labels.
If hunger or a worry rises, let it rise like a wave, and notice what it rises on.

wordCard.voice: Kahola. The one who asked Ushasta's question again, and heard about balya: childlikeness, the plainness that comes after learning, before the silence of the sage.

orig.note: Sanskrit bālya: childhood, from bāla, child. Shankara links it to bala, strength.

carryVoice: Keep this close: the self is beyond hunger, grief and death. Tomorrow, a woman stands up in the courtyard and keeps asking why. See you then.
